title: Professional Standards — APG, AGRA, BGS, ICG

subChunks.title: Professional Standards — APG, AGRA, BGS, ICG

storyBeats.txt: You have mastered the craft of genealogical research, Theodora said. Now we turn to the profession — and a profession is defined not only by what its practitioners know but by how they conduct themselves.

Professional genealogical organisations set standards for exactly that: what constitutes competent, ethical, and honest genealogical practice. Membership of these organisations signals to clients and colleagues that you are committed to those standards.

But more than membership, credentials matter. The BCG's Certified Genealogist. AGRA membership. The BGS Fellowship. These are not merely letters after your name — they are a guarantee to clients that your work has been assessed against documented standards.

And they are a commitment to continuing education. The standards of genealogical practice are not static. New records open. New DNA techniques emerge. New research methodologies are developed. A professional keeps learning.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Anyone can call themselves a genealogist. Unlike medicine, law, or accountancy, genealogy has no statutory licensing requirement in most jurisdictions. A person with no training whatsoever can advertise professional genealogical services, charge fees, and produce research that is riddled with errors — and the client has no formal recourse.

Professional genealogical organisations exist to address this problem. They establish voluntary standards, operate credentialling systems, and maintain codes of ethics that define what professional conduct looks like. Understanding these organisations — their credentials, their standards, and their ethical frameworks — is essential for any genealogist who wants to practise professionally and to protect both their clients and their own reputation.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Association of Professional Genealogists (APG)

The APG (apgen.org) is the largest membership organisation for genealogical professionals in the United States and internationally. Membership is open to any person working professionally in genealogy, regardless of credential level — the APG is not a credentialling body but a professional community. It publishes the APG Quarterly, maintains a directory of professional genealogists searchable by specialism and geographic area, and operates a robust Code of Ethics.

The APG Code of Ethics covers: honesty with clients about the scope and limitations of research; accurate citation of all sources; avoidance of conflicts of interest; confidentiality of client information; commitment to continuing education; and honest advertising of services and qualifications. Every APG member commits to this code on joining.

Board for Certification of Genealogists (BCG)

The BCG (bcgcertification.org) is the principal credentialling body for professional genealogists in the United States. It awards two credentials:

  • Certified Genealogist (CG): For genealogical researchers. Requires submission of a portfolio demonstrating competence in GPS-standard research, proof writing, client communication, and ethical practice. Portfolios are reviewed by panels of credentialled genealogists; applicants must renew every five years through continuing education.
  • Certified Genealogical Lecturer (CGL): For genealogical educators and lecturers.

The CG credential is widely recognised as the highest professional genealogical standard in the US and is accepted internationally. BCG also publishes Genealogy Standards (2nd ed., 2019) — the definitive codification of the Genealogical Proof Standard and professional conduct expectations.

Association of Genealogists and Researchers in Archives (AGRA)

AGRA (agragenealogy.co.uk) is the principal UK professional membership and accreditation body. Full membership requires submission of two research reports demonstrating competence; reports are assessed by AGRA assessors against professional standards. AGRA members are listed in a public directory and may use AGRA-designated letters (AGRA Member).

AGRA's Code of Ethics mirrors the APG's in key respects: honesty, confidentiality, accurate citation, and clear communication of research scope and limitations. AGRA is the primary body for heir-location practitioners and forensic genealogists working in England and Wales.

The Guild of One-Name Studies (GOONS) and British Genealogical Societies

The Guild of One-Name Studies (one-name.org) supports researchers conducting comprehensive studies of a single surname — collecting all instances of that name worldwide. The Society of Genealogists (sog.org.uk) is the UK's largest genealogical library and membership society; it does not accredit researchers but holds the largest genealogical library in the UK and runs educational events. The Federation of Family History Societies (FFHS) co-ordinates UK county and regional societies.

International Commission for the Accreditation of Professional Genealogists (ICAPGen)

ICAPGen (icapgen.org) accredits genealogists in specific geographic and record-type specialisms through oral and written examinations. It was established to address the need for specialist-area credentials beyond the general CG credential — particularly for Eastern European, Latin American, and other non-English record environments. A directory of Accredited Genealogists (AG) is maintained for client reference.

National Genealogical Society (NGS)

The NGS (ngsgenealogy.org) publishes the National Genealogical Society Quarterly (NGSQ) — the peer-reviewed journal that is the primary venue for model proof arguments — and runs the annual NGS conference, one of the largest genealogical education events in the world. NGS also publishes standards documents including 'Standards for Sharing Information with Others' (addressing citation and responsible information sharing).

Practical Career Path

A typical professional development path: join APG and the relevant national society → study and apply the GPS through the BCG's Genealogy Standards → build a portfolio of client research reports → apply for AGRA membership (UK) or BCG's CG credential (US/international) → participate in continuing education (NGS Conference, IGHR, SLIG, GRIP, British Institute of Genealogical and Heraldic Studies) → mentor others and contribute to the profession through society work, lecturing, or publication.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why genealogy has voluntary professional standards rather than mandatory licensing, and why those standards still matter for clients choosing a genealogist.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Compare the APG Code of Ethics and the BCG's Genealogy Standards in terms of their purpose and what they ask of genealogical practitioners. What do they have in common, and where do they differ in emphasis? How would you use both in establishing a professional genealogical practice?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Both the APG Code of Ethics and BCG's Genealogy Standards share a core commitment to: honesty with clients about research scope and limitations; accurate citation of all sources; confidentiality of client information; and ongoing education. Both treat the Genealogical Proof Standard as the baseline for research quality.

Key differences in emphasis: The APG Code of Ethics focuses primarily on professional conduct — the ethical obligations a genealogist has to clients, colleagues, and the public. It is a statement of values. BCG's Genealogy Standards goes much further into the methodological detail — it specifies in precise terms what constitutes adequate research, proper citation, GPS-compliant reasoning, and professional report writing. It is both an ethical and a technical standard.

In establishing a professional practice: the APG Code provides the ethical framework for client relationships, advertising, and conduct. BCG's Standards provides the quality benchmark for the actual research work. A practitioner would commit to the APG Code as their ethical baseline and use BCG's Standards as their methodological reference — testing every research project and report against its specifications before delivery to a client.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: You are a UK-based genealogist considering applying for AGRA membership. Research (or describe what you know about) the AGRA membership application process, the standards against which your research reports will be assessed, and what ongoing obligations AGRA membership creates. How does AGRA membership complement or differ from the BCG's CG credential for a UK practitioner?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
AGRA membership requires submission of two research reports — typically one narrative report and one shorter focused piece — which are assessed by AGRA assessors for: accuracy of factual claims; quality and completeness of citation; appropriate methodology; clear communication; and ethical conduct (particularly in relation to living people and client confidentiality). The bar is set at demonstrably competent professional practice, not necessarily the absolute cutting-edge of the profession.

Ongoing obligations: AGRA members must adhere to the AGRA Code of Ethics; maintain their skills through continuing education; represent their qualifications accurately; and not misuse the AGRA designation (e.g., claiming higher qualifications than the membership designation confers).

Comparison with BCG CG: the CG credential is internationally recognised and requires a more extensive portfolio (typically five to seven documents demonstrating a range of skills), assessed by a larger panel. It has higher prestige internationally and is the credential most commonly required for forensic genealogy or heir-location work in US-connected cases. AGRA membership is more specifically valued in UK professional circles and is the standard UK solicitors and probate courts recognise for heir-location work.

A UK practitioner seeking to work internationally — particularly in forensic genealogy or academic genealogy — would benefit from pursuing the CG credential as well as AGRA membership. For a practitioner focused on UK client work, AGRA membership alone may be sufficient, though the BCG's Genealogy Standards should be used as a quality benchmark regardless of which credential is pursued.
learningObjectives: Identify the principal professional genealogical organisations (APG, BCG, AGRA, ICAPGen, NGS) and their distinct roles.
Describe the BCG CG credential portfolio requirements and what competencies it demonstrates.
Explain the key provisions of the APG Code of Ethics and how they apply to professional practice.
Outline a realistic professional development pathway for a genealogist in the UK or US context.
commonMistakes: Confusing APG (a membership organisation open to all professionals) with BCG (a credentialling body requiring assessed portfolios).
Treating professional credentials as optional luxuries rather than as quality guarantees that protect both clients and practitioners.
Believing that credential attainment ends the obligation to continue learning — all major credentials require ongoing CPD for renewal.
Ignoring jurisdiction-specific organisations (AGRA for UK, ICAPGen for specialist areas) in favour of exclusively US-centric credentials.
assessmentCriteria: Accurately distinguishes the roles of APG, BCG, AGRA, and ICAPGen without conflating membership and credentialling.
Describes the GPS as the shared methodological foundation underlying all professional standards.
Demonstrates understanding of the client-protection function of professional ethics codes.
Articulates a coherent professional development pathway appropriate to their stated context and goals.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Credentialling body awarding Accredited Genealogist (AG) designations in specific geographic and record-type specialisms through oral and written examination.

Major institutes: IGHR (Institute of Genealogy and Historical Research), SLIG (Salt Lake Institute of Genealogy), GRIP (Genealogical Research Institute of Pittsburgh), BIGS (British Institute of Genealogical and Heraldic Studies, Canterbury).
The National Genealogical Society Quarterly — peer-reviewed journal and primary venue for model proof arguments; setting the de facto publication standard for genealogical scholarship.
Annual APG-specific conference focused on the business and professional development aspects of genealogical practice, distinct from research-focused conferences.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary difference between APG and BCG in their role within the genealogical profession?
options: APG is US-only; BCG is international
APG is a membership community open to professionals regardless of credential level; BCG is a credentialling body that assesses and awards the Certified Genealogist (CG) designation
APG focuses on DNA genealogy; BCG focuses on documentary research
APG is for researchers; BCG is exclusively for lecturers and educators
questions.correctAnswer: APG is a membership community open to professionals regardless of credential level; BCG is a credentialling body that assesses and awards the Certified Genealogist (CG) designation
questions.explanationHtml: APG admits any professional genealogist as a member and provides a community, directory, and ethical framework. BCG is specifically a credentialling body: applicants must submit an assessed portfolio to earn the Certified Genealogist or Certified Genealogical Lecturer designation.

questions.questionHtml: A solicitor in England is instructing a genealogist for heir-location work on a significant estate. Which credential would the solicitor most likely recognise as a quality assurance?
options: ICAPGen AG designation for Latin American records
questions.explanationHtml: AGRA (Association of Genealogists and Researchers in Archives) is the principal accreditation body for genealogical researchers in England and Wales, and is the standard recognised by UK solicitors and probate courts for heir-location and professional research work.

questions.questionHtml: Why might a BCG Certified Genealogist still be required to engage in continuing education even after achieving the CG credential?
options: BCG requires CGs to pass a new examination every year
Genealogical standards, tools, and record availability evolve continuously; maintaining competency requires ongoing learning, and BCG renewal every five years requires documented CPD
The CG credential expires automatically after two years without renewal
Continuing education is only required for genealogists working in forensic or legal contexts
questions.correctAnswer: Genealogical standards, tools, and record availability evolve continuously; maintaining competency requires ongoing learning, and BCG renewal every five years requires documented CPD
questions.explanationHtml: The CG credential must be renewed every five years through demonstration of continuing professional development. This reflects the reality that genealogical practice evolves — new records open online, new DNA methodologies emerge, new proof standards are articulated — and a credential that required only a one-time assessment would quickly become outdated.
